clinicalPearls: Intraperitoneal infection follows disruption of a normal anatomic barrier (ruptured appendix, diverticulum, or ulcer; ischemic, tumor-related, or inflammatory bowel wall weakening; or leakage from adjacent pancreatitis or pelvic inflammatory disease), and evolves in two sequential stages: peritonitis first, then abscess formation if the patient survives untreated.

Primary (spontaneous) bacterial peritonitis (PBP) in adults occurs chiefly with cirrhotic ascites, develops in up to about 10% of cirrhotic patients, and is thought to arise from hematogenous spread when impaired hepatic filtration and altered portal flow allow organisms to seed and multiply in ascitic fluid.

A peritoneal-fluid count of more than 250 polymorphonuclear leukocytes/uL is diagnostic of PBP; this threshold does not apply to secondary peritonitis. Normal peritoneal fluid contains under 300 WBC/uL (mainly mononuclear) and protein under 30 g/L.

PBP is typically caused by a single organism (often enteric gram-negative bacilli such as E. coli, but increasingly gram-positive cocci and ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae); recovery of multiple organisms including anaerobes should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis and a search for a secondary source.

Fever is the most common manifestation of PBP (up to 80%), but abdominal pain and peritoneal signs may be absent; nonlocalizing features such as malaise, encephalopathy, jaundice, or unexplained acute kidney injury in a cirrhotic with ascites should also trigger diagnostic paracentesis.

Yield of peritoneal-fluid culture is improved by inoculating about 10 mL directly into a blood-culture bottle, and simultaneous blood cultures should be drawn because bacteremia frequently accompanies PBP; samples are best obtained before antibiotics.

Secondary peritonitis results from spillage from an intraabdominal viscus and yields a mixed flora dominated by facultative gram-negative bacilli and anaerobes, especially with a colonic source; early death is driven by gram-negative bacillary sepsis and circulating endotoxin.

The bacterial burden of a perforation depends on site: a ruptured gastric ulcer (if not achlorhydric) causes mainly low-pH chemical irritation with a low bacterial load, whereas leaked colonic contents (pH 7-8, ~10^11 anaerobes/g feces) cause intense infection from heavy bacterial load.

Bacteroides fragilis, though only about 0.5% of normal colonic flora, is the anaerobe most frequently isolated from intraabdominal infections and abscesses and the most common anaerobic bloodstream isolate; its zwitterionic capsular polysaccharide (polysaccharide A) drives abscess localization via a CD4+ T-cell-dependent host response.

Of all intraabdominal abscesses, about 74% are intraperitoneal or retroperitoneal (non-visceral); most intraperitoneal abscesses arise from fecal spillage (e.g., an inflamed appendix), and diverticular abscesses are the least likely to rupture.

The liver is the organ most subject to abscess; biliary tract disease is now the most common source (formerly ruptured appendicitis), and pylephlebitis (suppurative portal vein thrombosis) is another route of seeding. Half of liver-abscess patients lack hepatomegaly, right-upper-quadrant tenderness, or jaundice, so liver abscess can present as fever of unknown origin, especially in the elderly.

Hypermucoviscous (hypervirulent) Klebsiella pneumoniae causes a distinctive community-acquired syndrome of liver abscess with bacteremia and metastatic infection of the eye(s) and lung(s), originally described in Southeast Asia and now emerging in North America and elsewhere.

Splenic abscess is rare but frequently fatal if untreated and often diagnosed late (at autopsy in about 37% of one series); hematogenous spread predominates, with bacterial endocarditis the most common associated infection and streptococci then S. aureus the usual isolates.

More than 75% of perinephric and renal abscesses now arise from ascending urinary tract infection rather than hematogenous seeding; concomitant obstructing nephrolithiasis is the most important risk factor (renal stones in 20-60% of perinephric abscess cases).
harrison.pathophysiology: Intraperitoneal infection begins when a normal anatomic barrier is breached and organisms normally contained within the bowel or another organ enter the sterile peritoneal cavity. Inflammation triggers an early influx of polymorphonuclear leukocytes followed by a prolonged phase of mononuclear cell migration, with the leukocyte phenotype shaped by resident-cell chemokine synthesis. In primary (spontaneous) bacterial peritonitis, a diseased liver with altered portal circulation impairs the normal filtration function, allowing hematogenous organisms to seed ascites; cirrhosis-related defects (low peritoneal complement, diminished PMN opsonic and phagocytic capacity, gut dysbiosis with overgrowth of Enterobacteriaceae, reduced Paneth cell defensins, decreased motility, and portal-hypertensive enteropathy) promote bacterial translocation. Secondary peritonitis follows direct viscus spillage; an early containment phase produces a fibrin- and PMN-rich exudate, and severity reflects whether spillage is chemically irritant (acidic gastric contents) or heavily bacterial (colonic contents). If overt gram-negative sepsis does not prove fatal, the host walls off persisting organisms and PMNs in a fibrous capsule to form an abscess; B. fragilis is uniquely able to induce abscesses, with its zwitterionic capsular polysaccharide A stimulating peritoneal macrophages (TNF-alpha, ICAM-1) and CD4+ T lymphocytes that secrete leukoattractant cytokines, while the alternative complement pathway and fibrinogen also participate.
additionalDifferentials: Primary versus secondary peritonitis (single organism without source versus mixed flora with an identifiable viscus source)
Pancreatitis versus its infectious complications (infected pseudocyst, pancreatic abscess, infected pancreatic necrosis) - fever, leukocytosis, and abdominal pain alone do not distinguish them
Tuboovarian abscess and other female genital tract infection extending into the pelvis
Perinephric/renal abscess versus uncomplicated pyelonephritis when fever persists beyond 4-5 days of therapy
Hemoperitoneum (especially in trauma) mimicking infective peritonitis
infectionMimics: Amebic liver abscess (cross-reference Chap. 230) - positive amebic serology in over 95% of cases
Candidal liver or renal abscess following fungemia, often unmasked when PMNs recover after neutropenia
nonInfectiousMimics: Acute pancreatitis without infected necrosis (sterile inflammation producing fever and leukocytosis)
Chemical peritonitis from a ruptured gastric ulcer in the absence of significant bacterial load
Malignant ascites or metastatic intraabdominal malignancy
Congestive heart failure, systemic lupus erythematosus, and lymphedema as noncirrhotic settings reported with PBP
additionalInvestigations: Diagnostic paracentesis of any cirrhotic with ascites and fever, with PMN count (>250/uL diagnostic of PBP) and culture of fluid in blood-culture bottles plus simultaneous blood cultures
Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT to exclude or identify a primary intraabdominal source (highest yield for abscess localization)
Chest and abdominal radiography to exclude free air signaling perforation (pneumoperitoneum) and to suggest liver abscess via raised right hemidiaphragm, basilar infiltrate, or pleural effusion
Ultrasonography (particularly useful for right upper quadrant, kidneys, and pelvis) and MRI for abscess characterization
Indium-labeled WBC scan or gallium scan to localize occult collections (indium preferred near bowel); PET scanning for resolution and availability

Serum alkaline phosphatase (elevated in about 70% of liver abscess - the single most reliable laboratory finding), bilirubin (elevated in ~50%), AST (~48%); leukocytosis, normochromic normocytic anemia (~50%), hypoalbuminemia (~33%)
Amebic serology and PCR to exclude amebic liver abscess

In CAPD-associated peritonitis, dialysate cell count with differential (cloudy fluid with >100 WBC/uL, >50% neutrophils, or >50% PMN with shortened dwell time) and concentrated dialysate culture in blood-culture bottles
Needle aspiration under CT guidance for culture in suspected infected pancreatic necrosis
redFlags: Free air under the diaphragm on upright chest film indicating bowel perforation with peritonitis requiring urgent intervention
Hemodynamic instability in suspected secondary peritonitis warranting surgery without delay for imaging
Persistent fever after 4-5 days of treatment for pyelonephritis suggesting perinephric or renal abscess
Polymicrobial growth in PBP-suspected peritoneal fluid signaling missed secondary peritonitis source
Liver abscess presenting only as fever of unknown origin, especially in the elderly
Hypervirulent K. pneumoniae liver abscess with metastatic eye and lung involvement
Splenic abscess with underlying endocarditis or hemoglobinopathy given high untreated fatality
harrison.prognosis: PBP carries substantial morbidity and mortality, reflecting its concentration among patients with advanced liver disease; reported in-hospital mortality was about 17.6% in a 2018 US cohort, and another series found 23% mortality at 30 days and 37% at 90 days. PBP recurs frequently, with up to 70% of patients experiencing recurrence within 1 year. Patients with PBP usually respond to appropriate antibiotics within 72 h, and delayed therapy increases mortality. In secondary peritonitis, early death is attributable to gram-negative bacillary sepsis and endotoxemia, and the urgency and success of source control - rather than the choice of empiric antibiotics - drive survival odds. Pyogenic liver abscess mortality averaged about 15% despite treatment. Splenic and perinephric abscesses are frequently fatal when diagnosis is delayed, so early diagnosis is the most important determinant of outcome.
pitfalls: Failing to perform diagnostic paracentesis in a febrile cirrhotic with ascites, as PBP is often subtle and abdominal pain/peritoneal signs may be absent
Misclassifying secondary peritonitis as PBP - the >250 PMN/uL threshold and single-organism rule apply only to PBP; mixed flora or anaerobes indicate a secondary source
Relying on cultures from chronic drain sites, which are not reliable for defining infection etiology
Attributing fever, leukocytosis, and pain in pancreatitis to the inflammation itself and overlooking an infected pseudocyst, pancreatic abscess, or infected necrosis
Most clinical treatment failures in abscesses result from failure to achieve source control (drainage), not antibiotic selection
Injecting barium when perforation is suspected (contraindicated), even though barium enema may occasionally reveal a diverticular abscess
Missing splenic or perinephric abscess because of nonspecific presentation and frequently delayed diagnosis
Overlooking polymicrobial urine culture, known renal stones, or sterile pyuria as clues to perinephric/renal abscess
harrison.severityClassification: No single formal severity score is given; the text frames disease along the peritonitis-to-abscess continuum and stratifies risk by setting. PBP is graded operationally by ascitic-fluid PMN count (>250/uL diagnostic) and by markers of advanced liver disease (serum creatinine, BUN, total bilirubin, Child-Turcotte-Pugh score) that identify highest-risk and worst-prognosis patients. Secondary and abscess-related infection severity is stratified clinically as community-acquired mild-to-moderate disease versus critically ill or health care-associated infection, which guides anticipated flora and management intensity.
